claims.claim: Anthropic states it signed the EU AI Act's Article 50(2) Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content as a provider of both generative AI models and generative AI systems.

Anthropic says Claude models launched on or after 2 August 2026 support machine-readable marking at launch, and that models launched before that date fall inside a transition period with retrofit still in progress.
Claude Opus 5, Anthropic's newest model, launched on 24 July 2026 — nine days before the 2 August 2026 marking cutoff.
About 190 organisations signed the Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content, recorded as 82 Section 1 signatories and 152 Section 2 signatories.
xAI does not appear on the Commission's published signatory list for the 2026 Transparency Code, and no public statement of refusal by xAI regarding that Code could be located.

On the separate 2025 General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, the Commission records that xAI signed only the Safety and Security Chapter and must demonstrate transparency and copyright compliance by alternative means.
The Code of Practice generally requires at least two layers of machine-readable marking, but treats a watermark alone as sufficient for free-form text because such text cannot transport metadata.
The Code of Practice sets 200 tokens as the pivot for free-form text watermarking, relaxing reliability expectations below that length rather than specifying a detection threshold.
400 tokens appears in the SynthID-Text Nature paper as a benchmark generation length for test texts, not as a detectability floor.

Anthropic's help page states no token count, no minimum length and no detection accuracy figure for the Claude text watermark, offering only the qualitative caveat that a very short passage leaves too little text for a reliable signal.
Breaches of Article 50 fall under Article 99(4) and attract fines of up to EUR 15,000,000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026, with a limited grace period to 2 December 2026 for the Article 50(2) marking duty on AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026.

The Digital Omnibus on AI was adopted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and entered into force on 27 July 2026, deferring Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 while leaving Article 50's 2 August 2026 application date intact.

Signing the Code of Practice creates no presumption of conformity; the Commission states that enforcement consequences attach to non-compliance with Article 50, not to the absence of adherence to the Code.
Kirchenbauer et al. report that after strong human paraphrasing a watermark is detectable after observing about 800 tokens on average at a 1e-5 false-positive rate.
A 2026 re-analysis reports SynthID-Text reaching a maximum true-positive rate of roughly 0.30 at a 1% false-positive rate when the text is only 50 tokens long, rising to about 85% at 400 tokens.

DIPPER paraphrasing drops DetectGPT's detection accuracy from 70.3% to 4.6% at a constant 1% false-positive rate, and degrades the Kirchenbauer watermark detector from 100.0% to 57.2% in the strongest paraphrase setting.
Jovanovic et al. show that for under $50 an attacker can both spoof and scrub state-of-the-art watermarking schemes previously considered safe, with an average success rate over 80%.

Zhang et al. prove that strong watermarking is impossible against an attacker with a quality oracle and a perturbation oracle, and empirically remove watermarks planted by three published schemes with only minor quality degradation.
A 2025 study of commercial humanizer tooling reports SynthID detection falling from 87.6% to 5.4% true-positive rate at a 5% false-positive rate after DIPPER paraphrase, and from 66.5% to 1.5% at 1%.

Seven GPT detectors misclassified human-written TOEFL essays by non-native English speakers as AI-generated at an average false-positive rate of 61.3%, against a near-zero rate for US eighth-grade essays.

Vanderbilt University disabled Turnitin's AI detector, calculating that a 1% false-positive rate applied to the 75,000 papers it submitted in 2022 would have incorrectly flagged around 750 student papers.

The Commission's own list of national single points of contact under the AI Act names authorities for only 8 of 27 member states, three of them still pending final designation, and carries a last-update stamp of 26 September 2025.
The European AI Office employs more than 125 staff and was recruiting 40 contractual agents with an application deadline of 8 September 2026.
No AI Act enforcement action, formal penalty or published investigation against any provider had been recorded as of 11 August 2026.
The CNIL fined Google LLC EUR 50 million on 21 January 2019, roughly eight months after the GDPR became applicable on 25 May 2018.
Current text watermarking schemes couple detection to injection, requiring the provider's secret key or a provider-side detector, which forecloses independent third-party verification.
The Code of Practice requires signatories to implement an interoperability solution for watermark detection by 2 February 2027.
Anthropic stated in May 2026 that its run-rate revenue had crossed $47 billion.
A survey of 50 generative AI image systems found only 19 (38%) embedded any machine-readable marking and only 5 used the C2PA standard.

The Commission states that Article 50 will mainly be enforced by national market surveillance authorities, with the AI Office holding a limited role confined to systems where the same provider supplies both the general-purpose model and the system, or where the system is part of a designated VLOP or VLOSE.
Shumailov et al. show that models trained recursively on generated data degrade, and state that it is unclear how content generated by LLMs can be tracked at scale.

Graphite's detector-based study estimates that primarily AI-generated articles accounted for 49.9% of new web articles in Q1 2026, near parity with human-written articles for five consecutive quarters.

Anthropic states that a detected mark provides a signal that content was processed by Claude but is not fully conclusive, and that lack of a detected mark does not mean the content was not AI-generated.
Google DeepMind states that SynthID watermarking is not built to directly stop motivated adversaries and is an important building block rather than a silver bullet.
Turnitin disclosed a sentence-level false-positive rate of around 4%, against the sub-1% document-level rate it marketed at launch.
